source: Acceleration as a Derivative
a = dv/dt = d²x/dt², and zero velocity at an instant says nothing about the acceleration.
Students think an object with zero velocity at an instant must have zero acceleration there.
Acceleration and Its Sign defined acceleration as the rate at which velocity changes. With Velocity as a Derivative in hand, that rate is one more derivative.

$$\role{acceleration}{a}(t) = \dfrac{\role[tiny change in velocity]{velocity}{dv}}{\role[tiny time interval]{time}{dt}} = \dfrac{d^2\role{position}{x}}{\role{time}{dt^2}}.$$ Acceleration is the slope of the $v$–$t$ graph and the concavity of the $x$–$t$ graph. Its units are $(\text{m/s})/\text{s} = \text{m/s}^2$. The velocity at an instant and the acceleration at that instant are separate facts: either can be zero while the other is not.

The derivative at an instant depends on how a quantity is changing there, not on its value there. A velocity can pass through zero while it is changing quickly, like a ball at the top of its flight: just before the top its velocity is a little upward, just after it is a little downward. The change from $+$ to $-$ happens at a steady rate of $9.8\ \text{m/s}$ every second, so $a = -9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$ (up positive) right through the top.
A ball thrown up at 14.7 m/s. At the top (1.5 s) the $v$–$t$ line crosses zero, but its slope, the acceleration, is still $-9.8\ \text{m/s}^2$.
A particle has $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 5t$ (m, s). Find its velocity and acceleration at $t = 1\ \text{s}$.
Differentiate twice
$v = -4\ \text{m/s}$, $a = -6\ \text{m/s}^2$ (speeding up in the $-x$ direction).
Both are negative: the particle moves in $-x$ and its velocity is becoming more negative, so it is speeding up.
For $x(t) = 2t^3 - 9t^2 + 12t$ (m, s), the particle is at rest at $t = 1\ \text{s}$. What is its acceleration then?
At rest, but accelerating
$v(t) = 6t^2 - 18t + 12 = 6(t - 1)(t - 2)$, which is zero at $t = 1$.
The velocity is passing from positive to negative: the particle is turning around, and the nonzero acceleration is what turns it.

Thinking that zero velocity at an instant means zero acceleration. If the acceleration were also zero, the velocity would stay at zero and the object would sit still. A ball at the top of its throw doesn't hover. Check: look at the velocity a moment before and a moment after. If they differ, the acceleration is not zero.
Same signs: speeding up. Opposite signs: slowing down.
